newsitem.title: USA: Lead prices set to firm up - Exide Corp.
newsitem.headline: Lead prices set to firm up - Exide Corp.

text.p: The western world lead market is to continue in deficit through next year, helping prices climb slightly, said Thomas Parker, lead commodities purchasing manager at Exide Corp.
Exide is the world's biggest lead battery maker, a market which accounts for over 70 percent of total lead consumption.
Parker forecast average LME lead price of 37 cents per pound in 1996 and 38 cents per pound in 1997.

"I still remain fairly bullish - I believe demand is going to continue to exceed supply," Parker told the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries meeting here. "I don't see new production coming on in the immediate future."
Prices will firm up as the winter car lead battery making season strengthens in the fourth quarter, Parker said.
Mined production was set to rise from 2.1 million tonnes in 1996 to 2.18 million in 1997, with consumption rising from 5.04 million tonnes to 5.153 million.
The western world market deficit will be 124,000 tonnes this year and 74,000 tonnes in 1997, Parker said.
Net metal imports from the Eastern bloc and U.S. government stockpile sales are due to fall from a total of 234,000 tonnes this year to 196,000 tonnes in 1997.

Western world primary lead metal production is set to rise from 2.237 million tonnes this year to 2.347 million in 1997, with secondary lead production rising from 2.445 million in 1996 to 2.636 million in 1997.

U.S. consumption of primary and secondary lead is set to rise from 1.6 million tonnes this year to 1.615 million tonnes next year. The U.S. will need to import 240,000 tonnes this year and 235,000 tonnes in 1997 to plug the domestic supply deficit, Parker forecast.

Parker noted production curtailments this year of 60,000 to 80,000 tonnes in Kazakhstan, 50,000 tonnes at Metaleurop, 40,000 tonnes at Hoboken in Belgium, 50,000 tonnes at MIM's Britannia plant, 85,000 tonnes at ASARCO's Omaha plant, 20,000 tonnes due to problems at RSR Corp's Indiannapolis plant, and 50,000 tonnes in China.

Production increases this year included 60,000 tonnes extra production from U.S. lead recyclers, 30,000 tonnes from Trepca in Yugoslavia, and 20,000 tonnes from the new GNB plant in Columbus, Georgia as it solves start up problems.
The weak zinc market - lead is often mined with zinc - has kept some marginal mines out of the market, thereby tightening the lead concentrates market, Parker said.
